shows.title: Kim Lim: Source
shows.description:
Kim Lim (1936–1997) was a Singaporean-British sculptor whose spare, exactingly carved forms in stone and wood have only recently begun to receive the international attention they deserve. This exhibition, curated by Bianca Chu, gathers sculpture, prints and photographs spanning her career, taking its title from a 1988 sculpture and using it as a lens on her whole practice: not a fixed point of origin but a generative condition from which forms emerge and return.

The show leans into Lim's close, almost tactile relationship with material. After 1979, when stone carving became central to her work, she developed a working method built on sustained observation of a given block's weight, grain and resistance, letting the carved line "widen and spread, deepen and sometimes disappear" as she put it. Works such as Wind-Stone and Sea-Stone II stage a meeting between the permanence of stone and processes—wind, water—that unfold over vastly different timescales. Alongside the sculpture, rarely-shown photographs from Lim's archive reveal the eye she brought to structures and rhythms in the built and natural world, material she treated as more than documentation.

The curatorial framing draws on Daoist cosmology—the Dao as inexhaustible source, the five elements as movements rather than fixed substances, qi as vital energy—to suggest how stillness in Lim's sculpture can also read as latent motion. It's a rewarding show for anyone curious about the postwar generation of women sculptors working between European modernism and Asian material philosophy, and a chance to see a still under-recognized artist's work in depth.

shows.title: Passed On (留痕)
shows.artist: Huang Bohan, with historical works by Dong Qichang, Huang Binhong and others
shows.description:
Passed On sets contemporary silver work by Taiwanese artist Huang Bohan alongside historical Chinese painting and calligraphy, tracing how motifs, poems and gestures move sideways and backward through generations rather than in a straight line of progress. The gallery's own description points to Dong Qichang reworking a centuries-old poem in his calligraphy and Huang Binhong looking to older masters even while forging his own idiom — precedents that frame Huang Bohan's practice of translating brush-based ink painting and scholar's-object forms into hand-hammered silver.

Rather than building a tidy survey of influence, the show is more interested in the small, human mechanisms by which culture persists: an inscription noting who a painting was made for, an object handed down and repurposed, a technique borrowed and bent into something new. It's a quiet, object-based exhibition suited to close looking, and a useful counterpoint to gallery's concurrent carpet show upstairs — both, in different ways, are about what survives handling.

shows.title: UFO: Universal Futurological Organisation
shows.description:
Taking its title from a work by Slovak conceptual artist Július Koller — whose acronym slyly stood in for "Universal Fantastic Question Mark" as much as "unidentified flying object" — this group show pairs Koller and fellow Central/Eastern European artists Vlado Martek, Djordje Ivačković, Kateřina Ondrušková, and Monika Žáková with a younger cohort working in and around Hong Kong: Angela Chow, Clarice Blanche Hu, Jocelyn Chan, and Andrei Pokrovskii. The connecting idea is small, individual gestures pushing back against the "totalising structures" — political, institutional, social — that quietly shape a person into a subject.

The material range is wide: Koller's playful "Anti-Happenings" stamp works sit alongside Martek's visual-poetry drawings, Ivačković's spare jazz-inflected abstractions, Chow's layered watercolor-and-wax surfaces, and Jocelyn Chan's handblown glass sculptures that treat glasswork itself as a language of memory. Clarice Blanche Hu's textured wall sculptures and Andrei Pokrovskii's theatrical, totemic dioramas round out a show that's less about a shared visual style than a shared instinct toward quiet, coded resistance.

It's an ambitious curatorial reach for a Sheung Wan gallery — connecting a strand of postwar Eastern European conceptualism to contemporary Hong Kong and diaspora practice — and worth catching for the Koller works alone, which are rarely seen in Asia.

shows.title: Nocturnal
shows.artist: Uri Aran, Patricia Ayres, Julie Beaufils, Sedrick Chisom, Carroll Dunham, Nat Faulkner, Sasha Gordon, Kenji Ide, Olivia van Kuiken, Heidi Lau, Jack O'Brien, Kent O'Connor, Trevor Shimizu, Michelle Uckotter
shows.description:
Nocturnal is a fourteen-artist group show organized by New York and Los Angeles gallerist Matthew Brown for David Zwirner's Hong Kong space, bringing together painters and sculptors whose work leans toward the shadowed, the uncanny or the after-dark. The roster spans generations and sensibilities, from Carroll Dunham's long-running, libidinal figuration to younger painters like Sasha Gordon, Sedrick Chisom and Olivia van Kuiken, whose work has been gaining attention for its blend of psychological unease and technical bravura.

As a guest-curated survey rather than a single-artist statement, the show functions as a snapshot of how a particular generation of American painters is currently handling darkness, dream logic and interiority — useful viewing for anyone tracking the artists likely to define the next few years of gallery conversation.

shows.title: Qi Lei: Echoes of Day and Night
shows.description:
Qi Lei's first show with Ben Brown Fine Arts pairs the Shanghai-based painter's figurative instincts with a strong pull toward abstraction, using music as an unlikely bridge between the two. The title comes from the artist's encounter with the instrumental post-rock band Godspeed You! Black Emperor, whose wordless, structurally abstract compositions got him thinking about how a painting can build rhythm and form without relying on a legible subject.

That thinking plays out most directly in works like "Morning Mist Rises at Dusk," where the painting's title collapses two ends of the day into a single, hard-to-place moment — dawn and dusk, sunrise and sunset, made confusable by nothing but changing light. Across the show, Qi Lei treats existing, recognizable images less as subjects to reproduce than as raw material to be dissolved and reorganized, worrying at the seam between a legible picture and the more abstract rhythm of paint itself.

It's a quiet, deliberately unresolved body of work — paintings that seem to be caught mid-transition, unwilling to commit fully to either figuration or abstraction, music or silence, night or day.

shows.title: Soft Borders
shows.artist: Igshaan Adams, Bi Rongrong, Kazuko Miyamoto, Angela Su, Aiko Tezuka, Yee I-Lann
shows.description:
Six artists from very different geographies — South Africa, China, Japan, Hong Kong, Malaysia — meet here on the shared ground of weaving, knotting and interlacing, treating thread and its relatives (beads, wire, bamboo, hair, enamel) less as a medium than as a way of thinking. The show's premise is that textile logic offers a useful model for talking about borders of every kind: social, cultural, historical, geographical, and the way all of them turn out to be more permeable and more constructed than they look.

Igshaan Adams, known for large tapestry-like works that map the psychic geography of his Cape Town neighborhood, appears alongside Kazuko Miyamoto, a former Sol LeWitt studio assistant whose string constructions helped define a minimalist, process-based fiber practice in 1970s New York. Bi Rongrong and Aiko Tezuka both work through the unraveling and reconstruction of woven and printed cloth, treating textile history as an archive to be picked apart and rewoven. Hong Kong's own Angela Su brings her long-standing interest in the body and craft-based labor, while Yee I-Lann, working from Sabah in Malaysia, continues her collaborative weaving projects with local communities, turning domestic objects like the doormat into pointed commentary on labor and value.

Taken together, the works suggest that softness — in material and in the borders under discussion — is not weakness but a different kind of structural logic, one built on negotiation and interdependence rather than rigid lines.

shows.title: Spillover
shows.description:
Ann Zhao's first exhibition in Greater Asia takes its title from a passage in the Zhuangzi about the different registers of speech and their capacity — or incapacity — to communicate the Dao. The word "spillover" does double duty here: it names both the productive looseness of everyday language (as opposed to fixed, formal speech) and the messier sense of contamination that occurs when one category bleeds into another — when a personal crisis compromises a professional identity, or illness undoes the fiction of an intact, purely intellectual self.

The heart of the show is Ben Ming Nian (本命年), an installation of twenty-four photographs spread across the gallery's upper floor. Rather than lean on the painting practice she's primarily known for, Zhao mostly withholds it — a handful of images reference an unfinished canvas or an abandoned motif, but the bulk of the material is deliberately unglamorous, almost aggressively ordinary. That refusal is the point: by declining to "furnish the goods" expected of a painter, Zhao turns a photographic record of her own inactivity into the show's real subject, pressing on questions about what art is actually for and what happens when an artist stops producing on cue.

It's a spare, quietly confrontational exhibition — more diagnosis than showcase — that uses the artist's own downtime as material for thinking about the use and abuse of art in a life.

shows.title: Halfway Across the Rubicon
shows.description:
Luis Xertu paints waterscapes, fauna, and male figures that never quite settle into a final state: he embeds real dried plant matter directly into the acrylic surface, so the works keep aging after they leave the studio, drifting from green to autumnal browns over months and years. The title nods to the idea of a point of no return, and the paintings on view — canvases like "The Waves," "Headspring," and "At the Ditch" — read like stills from a slow-motion film of bodies suspended between land and water, memory and decay.

Xertu, a Mexican-born, Rotterdam-based artist trained at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie, draws on a decade of theater and dance work in how he stages his figures: intimate, often homoerotic tableaux set against black-box-like backdrops of foliage and shadow. This is his first solo presentation at PODIUM after appearing in the gallery's group exhibitions in 2024 and 2026, and it gives a fuller view of how his signature technique — living plant material worked into paint — turns each canvas into an object with its own unpredictable timeline.

Expect large-scale works built around recurring motifs of climbing figures, waterfalls, and men entangled with branches and foliage, alongside smaller, more intimate studies. The organic materials mean no two viewings of the same painting look quite alike, which is very much the point.

shows.title: In Search of Lost Time
shows.description:
Kwai Fung Hin's autumn group show takes its title from Proust and its subject from the domestic interior — the overlooked textures of daily life that quietly hold memory and feeling. Eleven international artists, including gallery regulars Bai Ming, Pierre Boncompain and Matteo Pugliese, work across painting, ceramics and sculpture to treat the living room, the shared table and other ordinary domestic settings as sites where personal history accumulates.

The premise is a deliberately quiet one: rather than illustrating grand narrative, the works ask viewers to slow down and register small sensory details — the way light falls across a room, the worn surface of a familiar object — as a way of pushing back against the blur of contemporary life. It's less a themed survey than an invitation to look closely, in keeping with the gallery's long-standing interest in artists who treat everyday materials and motifs with sustained, almost devotional attention.

shows.title: Lucio Fontana: Spatialism. Pioneering the Contemporary
shows.description:
Curated by Fontana scholar Luca Massimo Barbero in collaboration with the Fondazione Lucio Fontana, this exhibition closes out a trilogy of Barbero-curated Fontana surveys that began in Los Angeles in 2020 and continued in New York in 2022–23. It brings the Argentine-Italian artist's Buchi (Holes) and Tagli (Cuts) — the punctured and slashed canvases that founded the Spatialism movement — to Hauser & Wirth's Queen's Road Central space, tracing the idea from its scandalous 1949 debut through to the shaped-canvas Quanta of 1959–60.

The show is built chronologically and thematically around Fontana's central gesture: puncturing or slicing the canvas to open what he called "an infinite dimension" beyond the picture plane. Alongside the paintings are rarer terracotta spatial constructions that blur painting and sculpture, and a group of bronze Nature sculptures — geodesic, organ-like spheres punctured by the artist's own hand, evoking planetary or biological form.

For Hong Kong audiences this is a rare chance to see a museum-scale survey of an artist whose 1960s experiments with the canvas as object rather than support quietly set the terms for much of the sculpture-painting hybridity that followed. The accompanying monograph, published to coincide with the show, is the first widely available introduction to Fontana's work in Simplified Chinese.

shows.title: What Remains to Be Seen
shows.description:
Myonghi Kang returns to Villepin's Hong Kong house with her first gallery solo in over two years, following a run of institutional exposure that included the Seoul Museum of Art and Château La Coste. The Korean-French painter, who has worked between Paris and Seoul for decades, is known for canvases that build up densely worked surfaces of flowers, fruit, and half-glimpsed figures in a palette that swings between bruised darks and sudden, saturated color — bambous, hibiscus, and peonies recur here as recurring motifs rather than tidy botanical studies.

Based on the title and the works previewed for the show, expect large oils — some pushing past two and a half meters — alongside works on paper that reveal a more exploratory, sketch-like side of her process. Kang has spent over six decades circling the same handful of subjects, and this exhibition is framed less as a survey of a finished career than as evidence of an artist still testing what she hasn't yet resolved.

For Hong Kong audiences this is a chance to see an artist whose reputation has been built mostly through European and Korean institutions get a dedicated commercial showing, staged inside Villepin's atmospheric Hollywood Road townhouse rather than a white-cube space — a setting that tends to suit the intimacy and density of her paintings.

shows.title: When the Surface Thinks
shows.description:
Yunyao Zhang works almost exclusively in graphite on felt, a combination that forces a very different relationship to mark-making than oil on canvas: once the graphite is worked into the fibrous surface it can't be corrected or painted over, so every tonal decision is effectively final. Trained in an academic tradition shaped by Soviet Realism and French Beaux-Arts methods, the Shanghai-born, Paris-based artist has spent the past several years quietly working against that training — pushing figurative source material (classical statuary, carved heads) toward something closer to abstraction.

This is a solo presentation under White Cube's "Inside the White Cube" banner, the gallery's platform for artists it hasn't previously represented, and it brings together two connected bodies of work: the large-scale "Connector" series, which reads as illusionistic abstraction built from tightly rendered surfaces, and the "Time" series, close-up studies of carved heads that treat sculpture as a subject for drawing rather than a reference point. Seen together, the two series make the case that Zhang's real subject is the surface itself — its capacity to register weight, light, and touch in a medium that offers no room for revision.

It's a cerebral, materially rigorous show, and a good opportunity to see a younger artist mid-transition, still working out how far a classical draftsman's toolkit can be pushed toward abstraction.
